description: Air Force veteran, 15 yrs cybersecurity, CISSP + ISACA AAISM. I build simulations and digital twins. I like to use Houdini, Blender, Isaac Sim, Unreal, plus OpenFOAM and other scientific tools. I treat sim output as evidence, logged and checked against a standard.
summary:
Terrain Surf is an interactive web app for planning and exploring a Marswalk with a rover scout. It combines NASA orbital imagery and elevation data, Perseverance science observations, historical atmospheric measurements, and regional dust records in a connected 3D environment and 2D map.

Users choose science destinations, inspect elevation profiles and slopes, and compare a rejected direct route with a gentler proposed alternative. They can scout the route, switch between rover and third-person cameras, review NASA observation images, record field notes, and export a mission brief. Guided tutorials explain the workflow and help users interpret historical conditions, data coverage, and planning assumptions.

Terrain Surf makes information from multiple Mars missions easier to understand together, helping users explore where to travel, what science to investigate, and which uncertainties need further assessment. It demonstrates how an accessible visual interface could support preparation for future human exploration.
details:
Terrain Surf is a web app that helps users plan and explore a science excursion on Mars with a rover scout. It addresses the challenge’s central objective: bringing information from multiple NASA missions into a localized interface that supports route planning, scientific investigation, and an understanding of environmental conditions.

The prototype combines registered orbital imagery and elevation data from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s HiRISE instrument with Perseverance science observations, historical MEDA atmospheric measurements, and regional dust records derived from Mars Climate Sounder observations. Two terrain fields near Perseverance’s landing region in Jezero Crater provide the current exploration areas. The 3D terrain, overhead map, rover position, and movement telemetry share the same coordinate system, keeping the views connected as users navigate.

Users can click the map to select a destination or plan an excursion to a science observation station. The planner evaluates terrain against a user-selected slope limit and displays route distance, elevation changes, sampled slopes, and estimated travel time. When a direct route exceeds that limit and an alternative is available, the app retains a red dashed rejected route alongside a green proposed route. This makes the tradeoff between distance and gentler terrain visible and understandable.

The rover lets users preview the proposed journey from an orbiting third-person view or a virtual rover camera. During a science excursion, users can inspect archived NASA observation images, record their own field notes, and export a mission brief containing planning assumptions, observations, and source references. Guided tutorials explain the controls, prerequisites, and progression from planning a first stop to reviewing regional weather.

Historical conditions add another dimension to planning. Users can inspect dated atmospheric readings, explore regional dust records over time, and compare historical departure conditions alongside an excursion plan. Dates, coverage, source resolution, and missing measurements remain visible. Both current terrain fields fall within the same coarse regional dust cell, so the app preserves that shared coverage rather than inventing weather differences between nearby locations.

The project’s creative contribution is the connection between an accessible driving experience and a scientific planning workflow. Users can move between an orbital overview, a ground-level perspective, route analysis, environmental context, and a sourced field notebook. This helps make separate mission datasets easier to interpret together and exposes the reasoning behind a proposed route.

Terrain Surf uses JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Three.js/WebGL, and Driver.js. Blender supported preparation of the existing rover visual for GLB delivery, Python supported verification utilities and automated browser checks, and FFmpeg supported editing the recorded demonstration. GitHub Pages hosts the static application at terrain.surf over HTTPS. AI assistance supported code and text development under human direction, with its use documented in the repository.

Items considered were scientific provenance, spatial and temporal coverage, browser performance, understandable controls, and uncertainty. Terrain measurements and archived observations remain distinguishable from illustrative lighting, virtual camera views, and planning assumptions. Rover movement uses terrain-following kinematics; calibrated wheel slip, soil response, energy consumption, radiation exposure, and weather forecasting remain outside the prototype’s validated scope.

The intended impact is to demonstrate how a visual, traceable interface could help future explorers, mission planners, students, and the public understand terrain constraints, investigate science destinations, and identify where additional evidence is needed.

Source code and documentation: https://github.com/MrHenriA/terrain-surf
